claims.claim: A wind turbine converts the wind's kinetic energy to electricity: wind flowing across the blades creates a pressure difference that produces aerodynamic lift, spinning a rotor connected through a shaft (directly or via a gearbox) to a generator.

The power available in the wind is P = 1/2 * rho * A * v^3, where rho is air density (~1.225 kg/m^3 at sea level), A is the rotor swept area (A = pi*(D/2)^2), and v is wind speed; power is directly proportional to swept area and to the cube of wind speed, so doubling wind speed multiplies available power by eight and doubling rotor diameter quadruples swept area and available power.

No turbine can capture more than about 59.3% (16/27) of the wind's kinetic energy; this theoretical maximum is the Betz limit, derived by German physicist Albert Betz in 1919, and real turbines fall short of it (common overall efficiencies near 35-45%).

Offshore wind tends to operate at a higher capacity factor than onshore wind because of stronger and less variable wind speeds, but offshore wind electricity is generally more expensive than land-based generation.

The U.S. onshore wind fleet's annual capacity factor was 33.5% in 2023 (an eight-year low) and 35.9% in 2022 (its all-time high), meaning the fleet produces roughly a third of the electricity it would at full nameplate output.
Wind supplied about 10.5% of total U.S. utility-scale electricity generation in 2025, roughly 464 billion kWh, up from about 6 billion kWh in 2000.

Key trade-offs of wind energy include its variability (output rises and falls with the wind), remote siting that requires new transmission, wildlife impacts, and noise and visual concerns; land-based utility-scale wind is nonetheless among the lower-cost sources of new generation.

As of March 2022 the U.S. had more than 135 GW of net summer onshore wind capacity, while only two small offshore projects were operating (Block Island, 30 MW, 2016; Coastal Virginia pilot, 12 MW, 2021), with more than 6 GW of additional offshore capacity planned along the eastern seaboard.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The word 'efficiency' is used two different ways in wind sources.
positions: The Betz limit (~59.3%) is the theoretical ceiling on the fraction of the wind's kinetic energy any rotor can extract.
Capacity factor (~34% for the U.S. fleet) is the ratio of actual annual generation to nameplate output over time, not an instantaneous energy-conversion efficiency.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps these separate: Betz is an instantaneous physical ceiling on energy capture; capacity factor is a time-averaged utilization measure driven mainly by how often and how hard the wind blows.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Reported wind generation share depends on the reporting year and whether small-scale (distributed) generation is included.
positions: EIA reports ~10.5% of total U.S. utility-scale generation from wind in 2025.
Earlier full-year data (2024) put wind near 10.3% of utility-scale generation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson anchors on the most recent EIA figure (~10.5%, 2025), states it is utility-scale, and dates it.

sourceRecords.title: How Do Wind Turbines Work?
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Energy, Wind Energy Technologies Office
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the energy-conversion pathway: 'When wind flows across the blade, the air pressure on one side of the blade decreases... creates both lift and drag,' with lift exceeding drag to spin the rotor, which connects to a generator directly or through a gearbox. U.S. government work, public domain; used as factual reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Advantages and Challenges of Wind Energy
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Energy, Wind Energy Technologies Office
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the trade-offs and the low-cost point: ideal sites are often remote and need transmission upgrades; concerns include turbine-blade noise, visual impacts, and wildlife interactions; 'Land-based, utility-scale wind turbines can provide low-cost energy'; wind provides more than 10% of the country's electricity. U.S. government work, public domain; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Wind explained - Electricity generation from wind
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the dated generation share: 'In 2025, wind turbines were the source of about 10.5% of total U.S. utility-scale electricity generation,' and total wind generation rising from about 6 billion kWh in 2000 to about 464 billion kWh in 2025. U.S. government work, public domain; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. wind generation and capacity factor (Today in Energy, Apr 30, 2024)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the onshore capacity-factor figures: the U.S. wind fleet's average annual capacity factor 'fell to an eight-year low of 33.5% (compared with 35.9% in 2022, the all-time high).' Data from EIA Electric Power Monthly and Power Plant Operations Report. U.S. government work, public domain; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Developers plan to add 6 gigawatts of U.S. offshore wind capacity through 2029 (Today in Energy)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the onshore-vs-offshore contrast (June 2022): 'Offshore wind tends to operate at a higher capacity factor than onshore wind because of stronger and less variable wind speeds' and 'Offshore wind electricity generation is generally more expensive than land-based energy sources.' Also >135 GW net summer onshore capacity (March 2022); operating offshore limited to Block Island (30 MW, 2016) and Coastal Virginia pilot (12 MW, 2021), with >6 GW planned. Figures dated 2022. U.S. government work, public domain; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Wind Energy - Theoretical Power of Wind
sourceRecords.provider: Jim Trepka, Kirkwood Community College (Pressbooks OER)
sourceRecords.notes: Open textbook (CC BY 4.0). Supports the derivation and relation: KE = 1/2 m v^2 with m = rho*A*v*t gives wind power = 1/2 rho A v^3; power directly proportional to swept area (pi*(d/2)^2), to air density rho, and to v^3; worked example shows 187.5 kW at one speed and 1500 kW at double the speed, 'an 8x increase in power for a 2x increase in velocity.' Relation re-derived and re-worded here; attribution recorded.

sourceRecords.title: Betz limit
sourceRecords.notes: Corroborates the Betz limit and its attribution: 'conjectured by German physicist Albert Betz in 1919'; the maximum is 59.3% (16/27) of the wind's kinetic energy; common real efficiencies 35-45%. Used only to confirm the value and attribution; no prose reproduced.
